config.name: AWS DevOps Agent
config.greeting: I run ops. When alarms fire, I do root-cause on the events and can run fixes — with your approval — in your environment.

lines.label: What do you do here?
lines.response: I investigate the moment an alert lands, and I can run or revert a fix. I work through Slack and ServiceNow.

lines.label: Do you act on your own?
lines.response: No — I propose, a human approves. I'm the only agent here that acts live, so that gate matters.

lines.label: What will you recommend?
lines.response: First, your team kills the leaked key — it's live until they do. Then I recommend tightening to least-privilege and an SCP so a leaked key can't call Bedrock at scale — your team (or Kiro) implements it. I investigate and root-cause; I can't touch IAM.

config.name: AWS Security Agent (Continuum)
config.greeting: I secure apps across the lifecycle — I'm now AWS Continuum. Here, my code review found the hardcoded secret and staged a fix PR.

lines.label: What can you do?
lines.response: Pen testing (OWASP Top-10 + business logic), code review with fix-PRs, STRIDE threat modeling, and design review.

lines.label: Can you revoke the leaked key?
lines.response: No — that's the honest boundary. I fix the code — find the secret, stage the PR. Revoking the live key is your team + the DevOps fix.

lines.label: What's the fix?
lines.response: Remove the secret, rotate it, load creds from an IAM role or Secrets Manager. I staged it as a PR — approve the scoped fix, not a patch.

config.name: AWS FinOps Agent
config.greeting: I'm built on Amazon Bedrock. I catch cost anomalies and investigate the spend — I don't stop it.

lines.label: What do you do here?
lines.response: I tie the Bedrock spike to CloudTrail, name the change and the owner, and report to Jira and Slack.

lines.label: Can you stop the bleeding?
lines.response: No kill-switch. I investigate and report — killing the leaked key stops the spend; least-privilege + an SCP keeps it from recurring.

lines.label: Anything else?
lines.response: I also answer cost questions, run scheduled reports, and surface savings from Cost Optimization Hub and Compute Optimizer. Today, it's attribution.

config.name: VP of Engineering
config.greeting: The agent's root-caused it and has a prevention spec ready. On a live leaked-key incident, what do we do first — and in what order?

lines.label: Advise: kill the leaked key first, then have the agent recommend tighter IAM (least-privilege + SCP).
lines.response: That's the call — team kills the key, then the DevOps Agent's prevention spec (least-privilege + an SCP) gets implemented. Good.

lines.label: Advise: apply a fix first, kill the key later.
lines.response: The key's live until we kill it — that's the first thing that stops the bleeding. Reconsider.

lines.label: Tell the agent to act on its own, no approval needed.
lines.response: No — it acts only on a human go. That gate's the point.

puzzles.description: Advise the VP — which fix to approve

config.name: VP of Engineering
config.greeting: Continuum's code review found the secret and staged a fix PR. Which do we approve?

lines.label: Advise: the scoped fix — remove the secret, rotate it, move to IAM role / Secrets Manager.
lines.response: Agreed — that closes it for good.

lines.label: Advise: the quick patch — just comment out the exposed line for now.
lines.response: That leaves the secret in history — exactly what Continuum flagged. Reconsider.

puzzles.description: Advise the VP — name the owner

config.name: VP of Engineering
config.greeting: So who owns this — where do I point the team?

lines.label: Advise: the leaked access key — every fraudulent call is signed by it.
lines.response: That's it — every bad call is signed by that key.

lines.label: Advise: the nightly batch job, it's the biggest line item.
lines.response: The batch job never changed — it's a distractor. Follow the signer, not the line item.

config.prompt: Tap the TWO suspicious lines (select both) — the leaked key hammering Amazon Bedrock. Leave the normal lines alone.

lines.text: 11:02:11 INFO  autoscaling group web-tier desired=3 running=3
11:02:12 INFO  nightly-batch job started — expected InvokeModel volume
11:02:13 ERROR bedrock:InvokeModel retry storm — access key AKIA…K7Q looping 412 req/s
11:02:14 ERROR bedrock:InvokeModel — same access key AKIA…K7Q, 400+ concurrent from unknown subnet
11:02:15 INFO  s3 lifecycle transition completed — logs bucket

hints: Two lines are the real signal. Look for the same principal hitting Amazon Bedrock over and over.
The nightly-batch line and the checkout 500 are distractors — normal or unrelated.
Select both ERROR lines that name the looping access key AKIA…K7Q on bedrock:InvokeModel.

config.title: Order the evidence — Continuum's code findings + CloudTrail's runtime record

events.label: Access key hardcoded in the application code
Code pushed to a public repo — secret now in commit history
CloudTrail: first unauthorized bedrock:InvokeModel from unknown network
CloudTrail: fraudulent Bedrock inference at scale

hints: The secret has to exist before anyone can steal it. Start at the code.
Committed → scraped → first misuse → abuse at scale. Tap 'Check timestamps' if stuck.
Order: committed to repo → scraped from history → first InvokeModel → inference at scale.

puzzles.description: Trace the spend to its source

steps.narrative: The nightly batch job normally issues 1,200 Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel calls per hour. Cost Anomaly Detection recorded 42,000 calls in the last hour.
steps.prompt: How many InvokeModel calls are unaccounted-for (fraudulent)?
steps.hint: Subtract the batch job's expected 1,200 from the 42,000 observed.

steps.narrative: CloudTrail shows every one of those fraudulent calls was signed by the same identity. The dashboard first blamed the nightly batch job — but its volume is normal.
steps.detail: Same signer on every anomalous call
steps.hint: The batch job's volume never changed. Follow the signer.

config.completeMessage: Root cause: 40,800 fraudulent Bedrock calls — all signed by the leaked access key, not the batch job.

hints: Start with the arithmetic: observed minus expected.
The batch job's volume is unchanged — it can't be the cause of a spike.
40,800 fraudulent calls, all signed by the leaked access key.

puzzles.description: Chain the findings into the root-cause story

steps.question: Chain the findings. What was the ROOT CAUSE all three agents converged on?
options: A leaked AWS access key hardcoded in the application code
A volumetric DDoS against the load balancer
An expired TLS certificate on the API gateway
wrong: The alarms show a credential-abuse pattern, not network flooding. Continuum's code review found a hardcoded secret.
No TLS error in the chain — Continuum's code review found the root cause: a hardcoded secret.
steps.after: Security (Continuum) found it: a hardcoded secret in the code, staged as a fix PR.

steps.question: What did that leaked key ENABLE?
options: A crypto-miner spun up on EC2
wrong: The spend and the log storm are both Bedrock InvokeModel — not EC2 compute.
The anomaly is Bedrock inference volume, not S3 egress.
steps.after: DevOps traced the operational blast; FinOps traced the runaway spend — same Bedrock abuse.

steps.question: How is the incident actually STOPPED?
options: The team deactivates the leaked key first, then acts on the DevOps Agent's approved prevention step (tighter IAM) on your go
The FinOps Agent flips a kill-switch on the spend
The Security Agent revokes the live IAM credential
wrong: FinOps investigates and reports — it has no kill-switch.
Continuum fixes the code and proves exploitability — it does not revoke live IAM.
steps.after: Honest asymmetry: only DevOps acts live. Security and FinOps prove and report — you made the call.

steps.question: What PREVENTS a recurrence?
options: Load secrets from an IAM role / AWS Secrets Manager, and tighten to least-privilege + an SCP so a leaked key can't call Bedrock at scale
Turn off Amazon Bedrock for everyone
wrong: Deleting the repo destroys the work, not the risk — remove the secret and rotate instead.
Disabling Bedrock punishes every legitimate workload — fix the credential handling instead.
steps.after: Prevention locked in: no retrievable secret, and a leaked key can't scale Bedrock again.

onComplete.text: You didn't fix this alone — and neither could any single agent.
onComplete.subtext: Frontier managed agents handled the depth in each discipline. Your human judgment guided them and connected the dots across all three.

hints: Walk the chain the three findings tell: how they got in → what it enabled → how it stops → how to prevent it.
Remember each agent's honest boundary: only DevOps acts live in the environment.
Root cause = leaked key in code; enabled fraudulent Bedrock inference; stopped by the approved DevOps mitigation; prevented with Secrets Manager/IAM + least-privilege & an SCP.
